newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Early Grozny count gives Chechnya's Maskhadov big lead.
newsitem.headline: Early Grozny count gives Chechnya's Maskhadov big lead.

text.p: Chechen electoral officials, working through the night to count ballots in Monday's presidential vote, said early results showed a big lead for the pre-election favourite, Aslan Maskhadov.

Such a result, and the very heavy turnout which caused long queues at polling stations, would send a signal to Moscow that the nearly million-strong Chechen nation wants free of Russia, but also wants peace after two years of bitter warfare.

The elections are a crucial step in restoring order and stability in the mountainous Moslem region still heavily scarred by 21 months of fierce fighting between Russian troops and rebel guerrillas bent on proclaiming Chechnya a fully independent state.

In a count which one official foreign observer described as "professional" and "enthusiastic", Maskhadov's lead in two Grozny districts would, if repeated across the region, give him over 50 percent and thus make a second round unnecessary.

The 45-year-old former Soviet artillery colonel is popular with voters not just for leading their tiny guerrilla army to victory last August but for the quiet level-headedness he showed in peace negotiations with Moscow in the autumn.

With votes from four out of five polling stations added, one of the constituency centres in the capital's Lenin district gave the chief guerrilla commander 3,382 votes to 1,125 for his nearest rival, hardline guerrilla leader, Shamil Basayev.

Acting separatist president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev had 481 votes. The total number of votes cast was not immediately available, but Movldi Basnukayev, head of the constituency centre, said no other candidate figured significantly. So Maskhadov may have won about two thirds of the total.
Basnukayev, observing the count in a damaged office building amid the bomb-blasted ruins of central Grozny, estimated turnout in his area at around 70 percent.

In Zavodsky (Factory) district, administration head Raya Gaytugayeva, told Reuters turnout in her constituency could be "over 100 percent" because large numbers of voters showed up who had not previously been registered.

The dislocation caused by two years of war with Russian troops has left hundreds of thousands of Chechens living in temporary accomodation. The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) provided skin-dying equipment to prevent double voting.

The ballot in Zavodsky district was even more heavily in Maskhadov's favour, with 2,247 votes from three out of four polling stations to Basayev's 421 and Yandarbiyev's 238. That would give Maskhadov a score of close to 75 percent.

Basayev is likely to do much better in the southern mountain districts around his home base of Vedeno. But the trend among voters questioned on Monday in the main centres of population and among war refugees bussed over the border from neighbouring regions was clearly in favour of Maskhadov.

A victory for Maskhadov would be greeted with some relief in the Kremlin. A win for Basayev, who is wanted as a "terrorist" in Russia, would be a nightmarish embarrassment for President Boris Yeltsin, who has admitted sending troops to crush Chechen independence in 1994 was a big mistakes.

All the candidates, however, are committed to turning the de facto independence secured by the withdrawal of Russian troops last year into full-fledged sovereign statehood -- something Moscow refuses to countenance.

Maskhadov has pledged to restore order to a region awash with weapons and to work with all the guerrilla leaders to avert Chechnya sinking into Afghan-style anarchy. He also wants Moscow to make good on promises of aid to rebuild the shattered economy, which was based on oil refining and pipelines.
